title: The browser is a separate computer
summary: Build an accessible form before introducing a Rust UI framework.
objectives: Explain HTML, CSS, DOM and browser events
Separate client validation from server invariants
Inspect a request across a process boundary
body:
Purpose: a trustworthy human boundary

A backend can preserve every database invariant and still be difficult to use. A person needs to know what can be entered, whether a request is pending, whether it failed, and whether a visible value is old. This lesson builds that human boundary before introducing framework machinery. Language knowledge and interface design are different skills; both need deliberate practice.

A plain model: document, presentation, behavior

HTML describes a document and its meaning. A heading identifies a section; a label names a control; a button performs an action. CSS describes presentation such as spacing, colors and layout. The DOM, or Document Object Model, is the browser's object representation of the document. JavaScript can read or update these objects and respond to events. An event is a notification such as a click, key press or form submission.

A webpage is not a screenshot. Its semantic structure matters to screen readers, keyboard users and browser behavior. A styled div does not become a button merely by looking like one. A native button already participates in keyboard interaction, focus and form behavior. Start with elements that express the action, then style them.

Predict before opening the example

When the focused quantity input contains 4 and you press Enter, does the form submit even if you never click the button? What happens if the input contains 101? Write your prediction, including what the browser does before our event handler.

Prediction explained

Enter can submit this simple form. Native constraint validation rejects the out-of-range input before successful submission. The script still validates its numeric domain because browser controls are not a security boundary. A different client can call the backend without this HTML.

Run a small, complete form

From the course folder, run mise run course, then open the quantity form. No Rust compilation is involved in this one exercise. It teaches the browser boundary that the later Rust WASM client must obey.

Read the unfamiliar lines

The viewport meta tag asks the mobile browser to use the device width rather than a wide virtual canvas. The label's for value matches the input's ID. This creates a programmatic name and makes clicking the label focus the input. The required, minimum and maximum attributes provide useful native feedback. They do not replace backend checks.

The submit listener receives an event. preventDefault() prevents this local demonstration from navigating to a new document. Number(...) converts text to a JavaScript number; Number.isInteger rejects fractional units. Assigning textContent treats the resulting message as text. Assigning untrusted input to innerHTML would parse markup and can create an injection boundary. The status region allows assistive technology to announce the updated message without moving focus.

Deliberate mistake: feedback that disappears

Remove preventDefault() in a learner copy. Submit a valid number and observe the URL and status. The browser's default form navigation can reload the document and discard the local message. This is a behavior error, not a Rust type error. Restore the handler or intentionally use a server-rendered form with a real action; both can be sound when the entire interaction is designed.

Guided checkpoint: label, submit, explain

Reconstruct the file in three edits: create the semantic form, add the numeric constraints, then attach the submit handler. Reload after each edit. Your checkpoint passes when a mouse click and Enter both produce the same valid preview, an invalid number has understandable feedback, and Tab visibly reaches each control. At 320 pixels wide, the document must remain readable without sideways scrolling.

Independent practice

Add a second field for a symbol. Decide whether leading/trailing spaces are normalized or rejected, and explain the choice. Make the empty state different from an error state. Test the page with JavaScript disabled and describe the resulting capability rather than pretending it still performs the scripted preview.

Hint 1

Define valid symbol characters and length before choosing an input attribute. Think about case normalization and how the server will apply the same contract.

Hint 2

Use a label and a short help message connected with aria-describedby. Keep error text next to the field and do not rely on red alone.

Worked approach

Accept 1–16 uppercase ASCII letters, trim outside whitespace, and report an error for an empty normalized result or internal spaces. Server validation must still independently enforce the accepted alphabet. An equally reasonable policy rejects lowercase rather than silently normalizing it; the important part is a documented, consistent contract.

Review: a button versus a clickable rectangle

An intentionally incomplete control might attach a click listener to a div while omitting keyboard behavior and an accessible name. That is a mistake to diagnose, not the recommended starting point. A native button expresses the same intention with fewer independent failure points. Use custom controls only when a native element cannot satisfy the requirement, and then implement the full interaction contract. Complexity here is not Big-O; it is the number of behaviors you must maintain.

Playbook investigation: the handler never runs

Observation: clicking Submit with 101 produces no scripted status change. Hypothesis A: the event listener did not attach. Hypothesis B: browser validation prevented submission. A distinguishing experiment uses a valid value, 4, without changing the script. If its status appears, A is weakened. Inspect input.validity.rangeOverflow in developer tools to test B. Disabling all validation would hide the clue; the sound fix is to explain the allowed range and preserve validation at both boundaries.

When you get stuck

Concrete next action

Open browser developer tools, inspect the element's label and validity, then check the console for the first exception. Report the exact input, whether submission or navigation occurred, and the smallest HTML file that reproduces it.

Further hint

Observe the Network panel. If there is no request, do not begin by changing SQL or database permissions.

Evidence and mastery

Browser interaction supports claims about this page in the tested browser. It does not establish universal assistive-technology compatibility. Independently rebuild the form, explain why client-side validation is not authorization, and diagnose a missing label and a reload bug without the solution. Record a prediction you revised.

Engineering decisions and evidence

The current interface contract is a local, simulated service client: semantic controls, explicit loading/error/empty states, bounded sequential polling and server-authoritative mutations. Leptos 0.8.22 is used because reactive Rust state is a learning objective; the course shell itself remains static HTML. Integer-cents formatting avoids floating-point price conversion, UUID identifiers use a maintained implementation, and ambiguous writes are not automatically retried. The WASM compiler check verifies target-specific APIs. The October 9 live Chrome checks exercised loading, empty/error states, orders, retained identity after connection failure, reconnect, cancellation and narrow layouts. The October 17 build record separately verifies the updated locked dependency graph and generated bindings. These are dated, scoped observations; the earlier browser run is not a new runtime test of every updated dependency. The October 17 runtime follow-up loaded these updated bindings in Chrome and repeated offline recovery, replay, orders, watchlist/filter and exact-identity retry checks against a fresh synthetic backend. The reference source is embedded directly and hashed by the course renderer.

An SSR client would be a reasonable alternative if initial content without WASM became a requirement. A push stream would require measured polling costs plus a bounded reconnect and slow-consumer contract. These are requirement changes, not corrections to an intentionally poor first design. Your checkpoint must include a named state transition, a failure case and the evidence that distinguishes it from a plausible alternative cause.

title: Reactive state has owners and lifetimes
summary: Use Leptos signals to connect owned state to browser output.
objectives: Explain Leptos signals, event closures and reactive reads
Bound UI tasks and avoid stale updates
body:
Purpose: keep the screen consistent with state

When a connection fails, the same state may affect a message, a button and a quote table. Manually updating unrelated DOM nodes can leave contradictory displays. A reactive model derives the visible document from explicit state and updates dependent parts when that state changes. It does not remove the need to design the states.

Choose one stable framework

The main Rust UI path uses Leptos 0.8.22 with its csr feature, compiled to WebAssembly. Its official documentation lists Rust 1.88 as the crate's minimum version; the course compiles with 1.99 and does not infer support for every feature combination on 1.88. A 0.9 prerelease existed during verification, but the course selects the stable series. Leptos lets the same Rust concepts of functions, closures and owned data appear in a UI while teaching a distinct reactive ownership model.

Client-side rendering (CSR) builds DOM nodes in the browser after the code loads. Server-side rendering (SSR) produces HTML on the server. Hydration attaches interactive behavior to server-produced HTML. Hydration requires server and client expectations to agree; inconsistent initial data or invalid HTML can break that agreement. This project's CSR mode avoids that extra boundary while learning signals. Its cost is that the interactive dashboard needs JavaScript and WASM before it appears.

Predict a reactive read

Consider a signal named filter. One view expression calls filter.get() immediately; another is a closure, move || filter.get(). Which expression can be re-run in a tracked reactive context when the signal changes?

Prediction explained

The closure provides computation that the framework can invoke while tracking reads. An eager call computes an ordinary value at that moment. A signal is not magic syntax that makes every prior string update. Learn where the framework establishes tracking rather than replacing every expression with a closure mechanically.

Runnable checkpoint: compile the real client

Working directory: the course folder. The browser target is additional standard-library support for the same compiler, not a different Rust language. Use mise to select the compiler first:

mise exec -- rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
mise exec -- cargo check --locked --manifest-path projects/ui-console/Cargo.toml --target wasm32-unknown-unknown

The full source is ui-console/src/lib.rs. Locate the signal declarations in App, then the closures in the quote filter and pause button. This is real Rust checked against the browser target; a native build alone would not verify the WASM boundary.

Explain the state model

signal(value) creates a read handle and a write handle. The handles refer to state owned by a reactive owner; they are not independent clones of the value. get() reads and clones this owned value when used for our small snapshots. get_untracked() reads without subscribing the current effect or computation. It is appropriate in a polling loop whose lifetime is separately controlled, not as a universal cure for reactive loops.

The move keyword transfers captured handles into a closure. It does not force every captured payload to be deeply copied. set replaces a value; update modifies it through a short mutable callback. Keep synchronous work in those callbacks small and never hold a borrow across an asynchronous request. An asynchronous task lives beyond the event handler's stack frame; everything it uses must remain valid until completion or cancellation.

Reactive ownership and Rust borrowing complement each other. The compiler can check ownership of the handle, but a framework-owned slot can still be disposed when its component is removed. The client uses an independently owned cancellation flag, checked after awaited requests, to avoid updating disposed reactive slots. Requests have deadlines, so cleanup does not leave indefinitely waiting work. Relaxed atomic ordering is sufficient for this one flag because it does not publish other shared data. Do not infer lifecycle safety merely from a passing native unit test.

Deliberate mistake: freezing a derived label

In a learner copy, calculate a formatted pause label once before the view and render that fixed String. Press Pause. If the button label stays unchanged, the backend and network are not involved. Move the derivation into a tracked closure. Avoid keeping both a boolean and an independently mutated duplicate label unless they describe truly different state.

Guided step: derive a filtered list

Start from snapshot as optional data and filter as user text. In the view closure, obtain the current snapshot, select quotes whose symbols match the normalized filter, and render rows. Keep normalization separate from the remote quote contract. A missing snapshot is loading or disconnected, not an empty market. An empty quote vector after a successful response is a real empty state.

Independent decisions, with tiered hints

Add a clear-filter button. Then display the number of visible rows. Decide whether the count is derived or stored. Finally, keep stale quotes visible during a temporary connection failure and label them as stale.

Hint 1

Ask how many independent facts exist. If a value can be calculated from the snapshot and filter, storing it creates another synchronization obligation.

Hint 2

A failed poll should update error/connection state without necessarily replacing the last successful snapshot with an empty one.

Reference approach

Derive visible rows and their count from the same predicate. The clear button sets the filter to an empty String. Retain the previous snapshot on a failed poll and show an explicit disconnected message. Add a last-success observation timestamp for display only; do not use browser time to order market events. Test disconnect/reconnect while a filter is active.

Playbook investigation: a filter appears to lose data

Observed: zero rows appear after typing “rust,” but the API response contains “RUST.” Hypothesis A: the server discarded the quote. Hypothesis B: the client compares case-sensitive strings. Read the Network response, then try the same letters in uppercase without another mutation. If the quote reappears, A is disproved. The smallest fix normalizes the search predicate consistently. Do not change server identifiers to satisfy a presentation-only filter.

When you get stuck

Trace one dependency

Write which signal should change and which closure reads it. Inspect the event handler first, then the derived view. Run the WASM check and read the first diagnostic before adding clones or extra effects.

Ask for a focused review

Provide the signal creation, one event handler and one rendered expression. Ask whether the read is tracked and whether its owner still exists, not simply “why is Leptos broken?”

Review, evidence and mastery

An explicit finite set of loading, loaded, empty, stale and error states is clearer than several unrelated booleans that permit contradictions. The demo still uses separate signals where the relationship is simple; an enum is a worthwhile independent refactor. Compilation supports API and type compatibility. Browser tests must establish that events update the DOM. Explain which work happens in Rust, generated JavaScript and the browser, then debug a frozen derived value without revealing the reference.

Engineering decisions and evidence

The current interface contract is a local, simulated service client: semantic controls, explicit loading/error/empty states, bounded sequential polling and server-authoritative mutations. Leptos 0.8.22 is used because reactive Rust state is a learning objective; the course shell itself remains static HTML. Integer-cents formatting avoids floating-point price conversion, UUID identifiers use a maintained implementation, and ambiguous writes are not automatically retried. The WASM compiler check verifies target-specific APIs. The October 9 live Chrome checks exercised loading, empty/error states, orders, retained identity after connection failure, reconnect, cancellation and narrow layouts. The October 17 build record separately verifies the updated locked dependency graph and generated bindings. These are dated, scoped observations; the earlier browser run is not a new runtime test of every updated dependency. The October 17 runtime follow-up loaded these updated bindings in Chrome and repeated offline recovery, replay, orders, watchlist/filter and exact-identity retry checks against a fresh synthetic backend. The reference source is embedded directly and hashed by the course renderer.

An SSR client would be a reasonable alternative if initial content without WASM became a requirement. A push stream would require measured polling costs plus a bounded reconnect and slow-consumer contract. These are requirement changes, not corrections to an intentionally poor first design. Your checkpoint must include a named state transition, a failure case and the evidence that distinguishes it from a plausible alternative cause.

title: Connect the operations console to a real service
summary: Compile WASM, proxy a same-origin API, and inspect loading, error and stale states.
objectives: Build and serve a real Leptos WASM application
Trace HTTP requests and response schema validation
Handle pending forms, reconnects and bounded polling
body:
Purpose: a complete request lifecycle

The operations console uses the same backend later examined in the capstone. You can learn its interface without yet understanding every trading invariant. The visible lesson is the lifecycle: user intent becomes a request, a server decision becomes a response, and the interface renders the result. At each step the client may know less than the server.

Plain model: four separate responsibilities

The Rust compiler produces WASM. The matching wasm-bindgen tool generates JavaScript glue that loads the module and exposes browser interoperation. A small loopback server serves these assets and forwards a fixed set of API paths to the local Axum process. The Axum process owns persistent state. The proxy is a learning convenience for one origin; it is not a general public reverse proxy.

An origin consists of scheme, host and port. Browser security rules distinguish 127.0.0.1:8011 from localhost:4116 even on the same computer. Serving the UI and forwarding its API under one origin avoids a CORS configuration detour. CORS is a browser access policy, not authentication and not protection against non-browser clients.

Prediction: a lost response

The backend commits a simulated buy, but the browser loses its response. Does the client know the order failed? Should it immediately create a new order ID and submit again?

Prediction explained

The outcome is unknown. A new ID can create a second independent purchase. A retry protocol needs a stable ID and a backend that recognizes that ID. This client's explicit error tells you to inspect the ledger before resubmitting. It does not silently claim failure or automatically retry mutations.

Build your own local-state checkpoint first

Working directory: the course folder. The immutable scaffold includes Rust source, its lockfile and an HTML loader. The project option selects the code you are editing; omitting it builds the complete reference console.

python3 scripts/start-project.py p11
mise exec -- python3 scripts/build-ui.py --project learner-work/p11-console
python3 scripts/console-server.py --project learner-work/p11-console

Install the versioned build tools shown below before running the build command. This first page has an accessible label and reactive filter text only. It does not need the API. Type a symbol, tab away and back, and explain which String owns the state. Stop that server before starting another server on port 8011. Later compare with the reference client or reconstruct its checkpoint in a different learner directory.

Run the complete reference console

Working directory: course folder. Use the exact bindgen CLI version matching the crate. A CLI installed by mise should appear in mise exec's PATH:

mise use cargo:wasm-bindgen-cli@0.2.129
mise exec -- rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
mise exec -- python3 scripts/build-ui.py
mise exec -- cargo run --manifest-path projects/Cargo.toml -p p16-workbench

In a second terminal, run python3 scripts/console-server.py and open 127.0.0.1:8011. The backend binds port 4116 and writes its teaching journal in the working directory unless WORKBENCH_LOG selects another path. Use a dedicated disposable lab directory for state. Keep the journal outside the portable course package.

In a third terminal, send one synthetic tick:

curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4116/api/ticks  -H 'Authorization: Bearer demo-operator'  -H 'Content-Type: application/json'  -d '{"event_id":"console-tick-1","symbol":"RUST","price_cents":12345,"sequence":1}'

The dashboard should show RUST at $123.45 after the next successful poll. Repeating the same event is a useful idempotency experiment; changing its contents under the same ID is a separate conflict case. These fixture identities are deliberately public local teaching identities, not a production login design.

Read the actual source

Reference implementation, reveal after tracing the request

Request::get creates a browser request. The Authorization header selects the local read-only fixture. send().await waits for browser I/O without blocking the main event loop. The AbortController limits how long a snapshot request may remain active. Parsing into a typed Snapshot checks the expected shape; it does not prove values satisfy every business invariant. Those are enforced by the backend.

The polling loop awaits snapshot, history and job requests sequentially, then a two-second interval. It does not create a new task every timer tick, so a slow response cannot accumulate an unbounded pile of snapshot requests. The history endpoint returns at most 60 recent event positions to this view, from a server history retaining at most 1,024 points. The LAB chart uses persistent event data rather than claiming each browser poll captured every tick. The text values provide an equivalent data view. The same page can queue a five-tick synthetic replay, inspect its persisted job cursor, request cancellation, edit a watchlist and inspect recent order IDs.

Deliberate mistake: inventing an empty success

Replace every fetch error with an empty default snapshot in a learner copy. Stop the API while the UI is open. The screen now looks like zero positions or zero cash rather than unavailable data. Restore a separate error path and retain clearly labeled stale data if useful. Default values can be dangerous when absence and zero have different meanings.

Guided checkpoint

Build the client, start the proxy without the API, and observe the error state. Start the API and observe reconnect. Add a tick and filter it. Submit one valid simulated buy and verify the next position/cash snapshot. Stop and restart the API with the same journal and compare the result. Each action crosses a different boundary; record which observation establishes which claim.

Independent practice

In your learner copy, independently reconstruct the watchlist editing form using the existing PUT endpoint, without copying the reference component. Preserve user input on failure. Disable only the relevant pending action. Provide field-specific validation while preserving server errors as understandable messages. Decide whether the control is optimistic or waits for confirmation.

Hint 1

Write the form's states first: idle, edited, pending, accepted and rejected. Include an unknown-outcome case.

Hint 2

Use the same-origin path and the operator fixture. Read the endpoint's exact JSON contract before serializing the request.

Worked design

A confirmed-update form keeps an editable comma-separated input, validates bounded normalized symbols, sends one PUT with a symbols array, and changes the displayed watchlist only after success or a fresh snapshot. On failure it keeps the input and shows the response category. An optimistic form can feel faster but needs a rollback/conflict model; use the simpler policy first.

Playbook investigation: the UI shows HTTP 502

Observation: static assets load but the snapshot fails. Hypothesis A: WASM cannot deserialize the JSON. Hypothesis B: the proxy cannot reach port 4116. The browser Network panel shows 502 before JSON parsing. A direct curl http://127.0.0.1:4116/health distinguishes backend availability from UI parsing. If connection fails, A cannot explain the earliest failure. Start the backend, repeat the exact request, then investigate schema only if the response arrives.

When you get stuck

Inspect the first broken boundary

Check generated pkg assets, browser console, Network status, proxy output and backend health in that order of request flow. Include one response status and a redacted body in the review request. Do not paste bearer credentials from a real application.

Review, evidence and mastery

A background interval that spawns requests without joining them is easy to write and hard to bound. A sequential loop has an obvious one-request budget. It can update less frequently under latency; that is an explicit tradeoff. Independently demonstrate disconnect and reconnect, explain why an HTTP success is separate from a durable business decision, and diagnose a wrong port without changing domain code.

Engineering decisions and evidence

The current interface contract is a local, simulated service client: semantic controls, explicit loading/error/empty states, bounded sequential polling and server-authoritative mutations. Leptos 0.8.22 is used because reactive Rust state is a learning objective; the course shell itself remains static HTML. Integer-cents formatting avoids floating-point price conversion, UUID identifiers use a maintained implementation, and ambiguous writes are not automatically retried. The WASM compiler check verifies target-specific APIs. The October 9 live Chrome checks exercised loading, empty/error states, orders, retained identity after connection failure, reconnect, cancellation and narrow layouts. The October 17 build record separately verifies the updated locked dependency graph and generated bindings. These are dated, scoped observations; the earlier browser run is not a new runtime test of every updated dependency. The October 17 runtime follow-up loaded these updated bindings in Chrome and repeated offline recovery, replay, orders, watchlist/filter and exact-identity retry checks against a fresh synthetic backend. The reference source is embedded directly and hashed by the course renderer.

An SSR client would be a reasonable alternative if initial content without WASM became a requirement. A push stream would require measured polling costs plus a bounded reconnect and slow-consumer contract. These are requirement changes, not corrections to an intentionally poor first design. Your checkpoint must include a named state transition, a failure case and the evidence that distinguishes it from a plausible alternative cause.

Reconcile a write before making another

A timeout describes the client’s observation, not whether a durable order exists. The reference keeps a PendingOrder containing one UUID, symbol and quantity. An uncertain response keeps that value and disables edits to the instruction. Retry sends the identical payload; Check exact ledger entry calls GET /api/orders/{id} even when the fill has fallen out of the latest-100 snapshot. A matching durable fill releases the pending state. A missing entry does not prove an earlier request cannot still finish. HTTP 408, 409 and server errors remain uncertain until reconciled; no mutation retries happen automatically.

This client retains an unresolved instruction only while the page remains open. Record the displayed ID before leaving or reloading. A production workflow that must survive browser crashes needs durable client command storage and a recovery UI; that is an explicit further requirement, not an inferred guarantee. Replay-job commands show their uncertain outcome and must be inspected in the durable job list before another job is created.

The native course-ui-model crate extracts transport schemas and pure decisions from the browser runtime. Its tests decode empty history with null cursors, distinguish uncertain HTTP outcomes and reject a sequence range that would overflow. These checks do not exercise clicking, focus or a browser’s network cancellation implementation.

The proxy admits at most 16 connections before starting handler threads and uses a five-second idle socket timeout, a 16 KiB request-body limit and a 1 MiB upstream-response limit. An idle timeout bounds waiting between socket activity; it is not a total deadline against a client that drips bytes. The server stays loopback-only. A socket fixture verified excess admission returns 503 and idle bodies release capacity; it does not verify browser behavior.

Retain a replay request across an uncertain response

A timeout does not tell the page whether the server committed a replay job. The console therefore keeps a ReplaySubmission containing the exact job ID and all five ticks. After an uncertain response, the button becomes “Retry retained replay.” A newer quote must not change those ticks: the backend compares both identity and payload when deduplicating. A later validation rejection cannot disprove an earlier successful request whose response was lost, so it leaves the original request unresolved. A successful response clears it. This state lives in the open page; reloading loses it. Copy the visible ID and inspect durable jobs before leaving.

Work through the investigation: suppose the first response is lost and the LAB quote advances before you retry. Predict whether generating new tick sequences is safe. In course_ui_model::ReplaySubmission, the retry branch returns the retained body before it calls the ID generator or reads the new sequence. The native test replay_retry_retains_identity_and_ticks_across_new_quotes_and_rejections supplies an ID generator that deliberately panics if called on retry, changes the quote sequence, and checks that the whole request remains identical through timeout, conflict and rejection responses. The intentional panic belongs only to this test oracle. It is not recommended application error handling.

From the course root, run mise exec -- cargo test --locked --manifest-path projects/Cargo.toml -p course-ui-model replay_. These tests verify the pure retry decisions. The separate WASM build verifies integration with Leptos types. Neither establishes browser focus, network timing or rendered behavior; those require the real-browser checklist. An alternative is persisting pending commands across reloads, which needs storage failure handling, expiry and identity reconciliation. This teaching client declares an open-page contract instead.

title: Rendering, security and alternative clients
summary: Review the interface boundary and investigate stale, inaccessible or misleading output.
objectives: Explain browser limitations and rendering tradeoffs
Design framework-neutral API contracts and an optional Svelte bridge
body:
Purpose: preserve the contract across clients

The backend should serve both the Rust dashboard and another client without moving its invariants into the browser. A new UI may change presentation and interaction, but it should not change what a valid order means. This lesson reviews boundaries and prepares you to evaluate frameworks without rebuilding the whole course.

Plain model: the browser is an untrusted participant

WebAssembly is executable code in a browser sandbox. It is not an encrypted vault for source, secrets or authorization rules. A user can inspect requests and bypass form validation. The server must authenticate an identity, authorize the action, validate input and apply domain transitions. The local demo tokens are public fixtures, chosen to test the read/write boundary. A deployed application should use a maintained identity system and established session or OAuth/OIDC mechanisms; designing one from a tutorial token is outside this lab's contract.

Cookies are automatically attached under browser rules and therefore require attention to SameSite, Secure, HttpOnly and cross-site request forgery. Bearer tokens grant access to their holder and can leak through unsafe storage or logs. TLS protects data in transit to an authenticated endpoint; it does not make a malicious client honest. The local course uses loopback HTTP for isolated fixtures. That is not a prescription for deployment.

Predict the rendering behavior

You disable JavaScript. Which remains readable: this static HTML course, the Leptos CSR dashboard, or server-rendered HTML? What part does hydration add?

Prediction explained

The course's authored HTML remains readable and its native details disclosures work. The CSR dashboard cannot construct its interactive DOM and shows a noscript explanation. Server-rendered HTML can provide initial content before JavaScript, while hydration adds interactive behavior. SSR alone does not guarantee that every form or control works without scripts; progressive enhancement must be intentionally implemented.

Runnable boundary experiments

Keep the console and backend running from the previous lesson. In the browser, temporarily disable JavaScript and reload both course and console. Then use the terminal to send a write request with Bearer demo-reader. The project’s boundary tests require it to be denied. Working directory projects/: mise exec -- cargo test -p p16-workbench. Read the authorization test and the handler it exercises.

Inspect a quote response without the UI. JSON is a serialization format: bytes describing strings, numbers, arrays and objects. It does not carry Rust's ownership information, and numbers can be interpreted differently by another language. The API uses integer cents and documented bounds; JavaScript's number type cannot exactly represent every i64 or u64. The pinned Rust client avoids a JavaScript number conversion when decoding: gloo-net 0.7.0 reads response text and passes that text to Rust serde_json. This preserves the Rust integer range or rejects an out-of-range value. We inspected that dependency's actual Response::json implementation; compilation alone would not establish this boundary. A JavaScript client that first calls JSON.parse can already lose precision before validation. The optional Svelte bridge therefore uses its documented lossless parser. Another valid wire-contract choice is validated decimal strings for large integers. Default small fixtures do not establish correctness at the representation limits.

Deliberate mistake: hiding a forbidden button

Hide the buy button when a client-side role says reader, but leave the server write handler unchecked. A direct request bypasses the visual restriction. The sound fix is server-side authorization, with the hidden or disabled button as a usability feature. Test both the visible role state and direct unauthorized HTTP request. One does not substitute for the other.

Guided project review

Trace a submitted order from its label and numeric input through serialization, proxy forwarding, actor selection, validation, domain transition, persistence and displayed snapshot. At each step name the owner, the maximum size and the error response. Record a table of which layer enforces each invariant. If the same invariant is validated twice, explain whether the client check is feedback and the server check is authority.

Independent client exercise

Design a second client that only reads snapshots and filters quotes. Keep the same HTTP schema. Describe how it presents loading, stale, empty and error states. Do not copy the reference UI's signals by name; write its state model first.

Hint 1

Framework state syntax changes; request identity, schema parsing and failure meanings do not.

Hint 2

Separate the transport function from the component. Test decoding with a fixture and an invalid response independently from click behavior.

Reference approach and optional Svelte 5 bridge

A second client should preserve the server’s identity, integer, resource and error contracts. The runnable Svelte 5 bridge connects to the same read-only snapshot API with exact integer decoding, bounded cancellable requests, a same-origin development proxy and tests. Follow its worked boundary investigation and independent watched-symbol exercise. Node and Svelte remain outside the Rust prerequisites; Leptos remains the main course framework.

The bridge pins Svelte 5.57.2 and Vite 8.3.4, with verified compatible tooling. It does not use SvelteKit. The shared backend needs no framework-specific domain changes.

Review: CSR versus hydration

CSR keeps the initial build path conceptually simple and works well for a local authenticated-style dashboard. Initial useful content waits for code download and execution. SSR provides an initial document and can improve first-content behavior, but introduces a server rendering path. Hydration must reconcile that document with client state, and both builds need compatible configuration. Decide based on the user's latency, accessibility and deployment needs rather than declaring one mode universally faster.

Playbook investigation: stale data looks current

Observation: the chart stops changing but the page still says Connected. Hypothesis A: the synthetic feed is stationary. Hypothesis B: polling failed but a previous status was retained. Inspect the latest successful request time and error path, then stop the backend intentionally. If the status still says Connected, A is disproved as a sufficient explanation. Keep last-success time and connection state distinct; a healthy transport can also carry old business data.

When you get stuck

Next experiment

Write two clocks: when the browser received the response and what sequence the server says it represents. Compare them during a stopped feed and a stopped server. Ask a reviewer to challenge the claimed freshness, not merely the CSS.

Evidence and mastery
